title: Six Ways to Prepare for Your Dental Visit
author: Precision Dental
excerpt: A little preparation makes a dental appointment run better. You get more out of the time, we get a clearer picture, and fewer things need chasing up afterwards…
imageAlt: A young boy smiling in the dental chair with two clinicians beside him
body:
A little preparation makes a dental appointment run better. You get more out of the time, we get a clearer picture, and fewer things need chasing up afterwards. None of this takes long, and most of it can be done the day before.

1. Gather Your Medical Information

Your medical history genuinely shapes your dental care, so it is worth arriving with accurate details rather than approximations.

Bring or note down:

  • All medications you take, including the dose, plus supplements and anything herbal
  • Any allergies, particularly to medications, latex or metals
  • Medical conditions, especially diabetes, heart conditions, bleeding disorders, osteoporosis and anything affecting your immune system
  • Recent surgery or hospital admissions
  • Whether you are pregnant or breastfeeding
  • Your GP's or specialist's details if you are under active care

This matters practically. Blood-thinning medication affects planning for extractions, some bone medications influence decisions around surgery, and many common medications cause dry mouth, which changes your decay risk.

If you are a new patient, completing the medical history form before you arrive saves time in the chair.

2. Note Down What You Have Noticed

In the chair, most people forget the very thing that prompted them to book. A note on your phone solves it.

Worth recording:

  • Which tooth or area feels different, and since when
  • What triggers it: cold, heat, sweetness, biting, or nothing in particular
  • How long the sensation lasts
  • Whether pain wakes you at night
  • Any clicking or tightness in your jaw, or grinding you have noticed
  • Anything about your smile you would like to discuss one day

Specific detail helps us narrow the cause quickly, which often means fewer tests.

3. Choose the Right Time of Day

Appointment timing affects how the visit feels. Morning slots suit people who would rather not spend the day thinking about it, and children generally cope better earlier in the day, well away from nap times.

Avoid booking with a hard deadline immediately afterwards, as watching the clock adds pressure to what should be an unhurried appointment. If you are having treatment with anaesthetic, remember your lip and tongue may be numb for a couple of hours, which can make an important meeting awkward.

4. Sort Out the Practical Details Beforehand

A few minutes of admin removes friction on the day:

  • Bring your health fund card so we can process your claim on the spot through HICAPS
  • Check your remaining annual limits with your fund if significant treatment is planned
  • Bring your Medicare card if your child may be eligible under the Child Dental Benefits Schedule
  • Ask us for a written quote in advance if you would like to consider costs before committing
  • Check our Prices and Payment Options page if you would like to understand payment methods and plans
  • Allow time for parking, although free on-site parking makes this straightforward at our practice

5. Say if You Feel Anxious

This is the single most useful thing a nervous patient can do. Telling our team when you book changes how the appointment is set up: longer appointment time, a slower pace, clear explanations before each step, and an agreed signal to pause.

You can also ask for a consultation with no treatment at all, which many of our anxious patients find a helpful first step. If you would like to bring headphones or a support person, both are welcome.

6. Prepare Children in the Right Way

For children's dentistry visits, how you frame the appointment matters more than anything that happens in the chair.

  • Keep the language neutral and positive. Avoid words such as needle, drill, hurt or pain, even when reassuring
  • Say the dentist is going to count their teeth and check they are strong
  • Read a picture book about visiting the dentist beforehand
  • Avoid promising there will be no treatment, since you cannot know that
  • Bring a favourite toy if it helps
  • Let us lead the conversation in the room, using language we know works with children

If your child has additional needs, tell us when booking so we can plan the visit around them.

A Few Simple Habits That Help

  • Confirm your appointment the day before, and ask us for an SMS reminder if that helps you keep track
  • Arrive a few minutes early, especially as a new patient, so forms are not rushed
  • Have something light to eat beforehand. It helps many people feel steadier, and if part of your mouth is numbed afterwards, eating can be awkward for a couple of hours
  • Give your teeth a normal brush before you come in if you can. It is appreciated, but do not worry if you cannot
  • If your treatment needs follow-up, such as reviews for new dentures, whitening top-ups, or fitting appointments for veneers or crowns, book those visits at the same time so they fit around your schedule

What to Skip

Two small things worth avoiding. Do not scrub your teeth unusually hard just before your appointment in the hope of hiding a few missed weeks; sore gums make the clean less comfortable and we will see the picture regardless. And there is no need to apologise for how long it has been. It is not something we comment on.

On the Day

Arrive a few minutes early, hand over your health fund card and medical information, and bring your notes. If anything changes between booking and the appointment, including illness or a new medication, let us know when you arrive.

After the Appointment

A little follow-through keeps everything on track. Book any recommended treatment before you leave, while the plan is fresh and the diary is in front of you, and take the written quote with you.

If you were given post-treatment instructions, follow them for the first 24 hours in particular, and keep the practice number handy in case something does not feel right. Most issues after treatment are minor and quickly resolved, but they are much easier to sort out early.

Finally, put your next recommended visit in your calendar rather than relying on a reminder arriving at a convenient moment. People who keep to their interval consistently need less treatment over time, which is the whole point of the exercise.

Book Your Next Appointment

Whether you are due for a check-up and clean or have something specific you would like looked at, our team will help you find a suitable time. Contact Precision Dental on {{site:phone}} or book online.

faq.q: What should I bring to my appointment?
a: Your health fund card, your Medicare card if a child may be eligible for benefits, a list of your medications, and any notes about what you have noticed.

faq.q: Do I need to fill in forms beforehand?
a: New patients complete a medical history form. Doing it before you arrive saves time and means we have accurate details from the start.
A few minutes is enough. Free on-site parking at HQ South Tower means you do not need to allow extra time to find a space.

faq.q: Should I eat before my appointment?
a: For a routine check-up it makes no difference. If you are having treatment with anaesthetic, a light meal beforehand is sensible, as you may need to wait for numbness to wear off.

faq.q: Can I bring my children with me?
a: Yes, although appointments run more smoothly if someone can supervise them. If they are due themselves, we can often schedule family members close together.

faq.q: What if I need to cancel?
a: Let us know as early as you can so the time can be offered to someone else. A quick phone call is all that is needed.
